title: Motoko Conditionals and Type Annotations
section: 38. Build Your First Defi (Decentralised Finance) DApp - DBANK
summary: Fixes the Nat underflow bug in withdraw using an if/else, and explains why an explicit Int type annotation on the subtraction result is needed. Shows that Motoko control flow looks like JavaScript.

concepts.heading: The bug being fixed
points: currentValue is a Nat, so it cannot go below zero. Withdrawing 999 from a balance of 100 raises a 'Natural subtraction underflow' error and the call fails.
The fix is a guard: only subtract when the result would stay at or above zero.

concepts.heading: if / else syntax
points: Conditionals resemble JavaScript: `if (condition) { ... } else { ... }`. Comparison operators such as >= work as expected.
Inside the if branch: subtract the amount from currentValue and print the new balance.
The else branch prints a message for the developer instead of changing anything. Because that message is plain Text, it needs no debug_show.
Statement blocks end with semicolons, including after the closing brace of the whole if/else.

concepts.heading: Why a type annotation is needed
points: Writing `(currentValue - amount) >= 0` directly produces a yellow warning that the operator may trap or that the inferred type is Nat. A subtraction of two Nats can't be negative in the type system, so the comparison to 0 is not meaningful as typed.

Fix: state the type of the result. It can be done in a separate constant: `let tempValue : Int = currentValue - amount;` where Int is any whole number, positive or negative. Then compare tempValue >= 0.
The syntax for an annotation is `name : Type`, the same style as function parameters (amount : Nat).
The reference solution also shows the inline form: `((currentValue - amount) : Int >= 0)`, annotating inside the condition without a temp constant.
Types so far: amount is Nat, currentValue is Nat (inferred from a positive literal, though it can be spelled out), tempValue is Int. A positive integer literal defaults to Nat.

concepts.heading: Result
points: A large withdrawal no longer crashes: the call succeeds, the balance is untouched, and the else message prints.
A reasonable withdrawal (e.g. 10 from 100) subtracts normally.
Takeaway: most language features carry over from other languages; the type system and canister interactions are what differ.

task.name: Add an else branch for oversized withdrawals
task.starting_point: withdraw subtracts the amount with a guard on tempValue but has no else branch.
task.goal: Print a helpful message when the requested amount exceeds the balance.
steps: Add an else block to the if statement.
Inside it call Debug.print with a text message (no debug_show needed for text).
Redeploy, call withdraw with a large number in Candid UI, and confirm the message appears and the balance is unchanged.
task.expected_result: Large withdrawal: message printed, no error. Normal withdrawal: balance reduced.

pitfalls: Comparing a Nat subtraction to 0 without annotating the result type.
Using debug_show on plain text (unneeded) or forgetting it on numbers.
Missing semicolon after the if/else block.
(Extra) The reference repo's message contains a typo ('currnet'); fix when copying.
